L’idée d’organiser une soirée de dialogu: The idea of hosting a dialogue evening on Palestinian pain came to me while I was preparing an article, when I realized I hadn’t explored this essential aspect in my interviews. In our meetings with Palestinians, many shared that their pain was often absent from media narratives.
Cette initiative a été rendue possible g: This initiative was made possible by the Palestinians who wanted their voices to be heard and who trusted La Converse.
Au cours des mois qui ont suivi,<em> La: Over the following months, La Converse met with members of the Palestinian community to listen to their concerns and build an atmosphere of trust. The process took time, but it was essential to create a space where this pain could be heard.
Les Palestiniens présents lors de cette: The Palestinians who attended this dialogue evening voiced a shared feeling: “Everyone talks about Palestine, but no one talks about Palestinians.”
Merci à nos invités d’avoir généreusemen: Thank you to our guests for generously sharing their stories in this article and the accompanying video.
Par une douce nuit de novembre, six Pale: On a mild November night, six Palestinians gather in our warmly lit studios to open up to La Converse. A circle is formed with floor cushions and chairs, for those whose knees have travelled too many kilometres to sit on the floor.
Imad, Nafisa, Fouad, Neda, Arwa et Asma: Imad, Nafisa, Fouad, Neda, Arwa and Asma all grew up a little differently. Together, they represent three generations and have lived in a dozen countries. Although their experiences, personalities and opinions differ, their stories have things in common. All of them ended up settling in Canada, but all of them hope to return to Palestine, even if only for a day. All share the same frustration at the neglect of their pain. All are deeply affected by the violence ravaging their homeland.
Ils sont tous d’accord sur une chose : «: They agree on one thing: “the voices of Palestinians must be heard.” That is why, despite fearing repercussions, they are speaking out today – for their children, for other Palestinians, for the whole world – and for themselves. We begin by asking the participants to introduce themselves, and their stories pour out almost immediately.
« Ma maison est là, pourquoi n’y suis-je: “My home is right there, why am I not there?”
Nafisa est une Palestinienne de 78 ans q: Nafisa is a 78-year-old Palestinian who speaks animatedly and smiles often, especially when she fondly talks about her grandchildren and her work as a translator. She tells us how her family was forced to leave their multigenerational home in Ramallah during the Nakba of 1948.
« La Nakba, qui signifie « catastrophe »: “The Nakba, which means ‘catastrophe’ in Arabic, refers to the mass displacement and dispossession of Palestinians during the 1948 Arab-Israeli war. Before the Nakba, Palestine was a multiethnic and multicultural society. (...) The Nakba had a profound impact on the Palestinian people, who lost their homes, their land and their way of life,” summarizes the <l1>United Nations website</l1>.
Les moindres détails de l’histoire de la: The smallest details of the Nakba are etched in Nafisa’s memory: the rigid barrel of a rifle pressed into her grandfather’s chest, then turned on her mother when she tries to go back into the house to get money; Israeli soldiers shooting at the olive trees, their branches falling on the heads of family members as they flee… Nafisa is only three years old at the time.
« C’est l’histoire de ma mère. Elle la r: “It’s my mother’s story. She told it day and night, every day,” she says. Nafisa and her siblings are tossed around within Palestine, and the family is scattered and pieced back together, until they all end up in Egypt. Meanwhile, her parents keep hoping to one day return to their homeland.
« Ma mère et mon père sont décédés en es: “My mother and father died hoping they would one day return to Ramallah” - Nafisa.
Nafisa raconte que, lorsque sa sœur s’es: Nafisa says that when her sister got engaged to an Egyptian, her father lamented: “Oh, how can I give her to an Egyptian? We will go back to Palestine and we’ll leave her here! No!” Nafisa remembers people telling him he was deluding himself in thinking he would return to his country.
« Ma mère et mon père sont décédés en es: “My mother and father died hoping they would one day return to Ramallah,” confides Nafisa. She managed to go back to Ramallah about ten years ago with her children and her husband. People told her it would be a wonderful experience. But for her, going back to the home of her childhood, where she would never live again, was deeply painful.
« Lorsque nous sommes arrivés [dans la d: “When we arrived [at the home of my childhood], we saw a Jewish man living in our house. My husband said: ‘Let’s knock on the door. Maybe he’ll let us in.’ When he said those words, I collapsed. I fell to the ground and cried my eyes out. He put me in the car, and we went to the centre of Ramallah, where we saw the places where [the rest of] my family used to live. They were all taken by the Israelis,” says Nafisa.
Son visage radieux s’assombrit à ce souv: Her radiant face darkens at the memory. “It’s as if all the feelings that had been tucked away came back… My home is right there, why am I not there?” Nafisa asks. Living in other countries never gave her the feeling of being at home. “It’s not just in the West; when you’re a stateless person in Egypt or Saudi Arabia, you feel alone… When you live as a stateless person, with no embassy for you, no one to support you, you feel like you’re nothing,” Nafisa laments.*

She says her education was her salvation, allowing her to succeed in countries where she was seen as a foreigner, having always felt like one in Egypt, in Saudi Arabia and, finally, in Canada.
« Lorsqu’on est une diplômée universitai: “When you’re a university graduate, you’re a rarity as a woman,” says Nafisa, recalling her life as a young adult in the Middle East. “So you’re educated. You do very well. You work very hard. But no one sees you as a first-class citizen,” she laments.
<em>« Voir les enfants de Gaza courir da: “Seeing the children of Gaza running in the streets and being bombed brought my trauma back, because we are children of war”
Fouad, qui est assis à côté de Nafisa, a: Fouad, who is sitting next to Nafisa, also lived through the Nakba of 1948, at the age of four. The elder speaks with poise and draws on his vast knowledge of history and the political events he has lived through, citing bills and politicians, attaching a bibliography to his personal story, beliefs and feelings.
Il est né à Haïfa, ville qui fait aujour: He was born in Haifa, a city that is now part of Israel, in a house on a street that bears his family’s name: Sahyoun Street. At first, his grandfather, who was deputy mayor of Haifa for more than a decade, told his family not to worry about the growing tensions in the region. But one day, violence came knocking at their door.
« Lorsque le cousin de ma mère est venu: “When my mother’s cousin came to bring us food, he was shot and died in front of our house. That’s when my grandfather told his children [to flee],” says Fouad. Fouad’s father drove him and his one-year-old brother to his grandparents’ house in Beirut. On the way, his father stopped at the bank to withdraw money to pay back a loan. “That’s an indication to show you the state of mind they were in. They never imagined they wouldn’t be allowed to come home. All my uncles were making fun of my father at the time,” says Fouad, showing humour in the face of a grim situation.
« Vous êtes venus envahir un pays très p: “You came to invade a very peaceful country where Jews, Christians and Muslims lived together very peacefully. You came with weapons instead of buying property, you drove people out.” - Fouad
Sa famille s’est finalement installée en: His family eventually settled in Egypt in March 1948. “Obviously, we were never able to go back, until we became Canadian citizens,” explains Fouad.
Sa femme, ses enfants et lui sont devenu: He, his wife and their children became Canadians in 1994 and returned to Palestine in the late 1990s. A 2011 documentary titled Fouad’s Dream follows one of Fouad’s trips to Palestine, during which he returns to his childhood home and reflects on the history of the region.
Fouad profite de cette soirée de dialogu: Fouad uses this dialogue evening to send a message to the Canadian public: “The partition of Palestine was a historic mistake, in the context of the colonial era of the British Empire. The French and the English were carving up the whole world at the time… You came to invade a very peaceful country where Jews, Christians and Muslims lived together very peacefully. You came with weapons instead of buying property, you drove people out,” he says.
« Ce n’est pas une histoire vieille d’un: “This is not a year-old story. These are truths we must express and tell people, and we have the means to do it. Personally, seeing the children of Gaza running in the streets and being bombed brought my trauma back, because we are children of war,” confides Fouad, his grand orator’s sweep fading as his voice breaks with emotion.
<em>« Moi, ma génération et mes enfants: “Me, my generation and my children keep seeing these disappointments caused by the Arab armies, the Arab regimes, the international community, the United Nations, human rights. It’s a series of disappointments.”
Imad est une génération plus jeune que F: Imad is a generation younger than Fouad and Nafisa, but their stories share displacement, the disappointed hope of return and a brutal exposure to violence at a young age. Imad also shares Fouad’s tendency to cite intellectuals and politicians, while telling his story in a tone that is both gentle and intense.
Les parents d’Imad ont vécu la Nakba de: Imad’s parents lived through the Nakba of 1948, which led him to spend his childhood in a refugee camp in Lebanon.
« Quand on est enfant, on n’a pas vraime: “When you’re a child, you’re not really aware of the real problems. You just play and go to school. I went to a UNRWA school. I think my first shock, my first passage into adulthood, so to speak, was the 1967 war. I must have been in Grade 3 at the time, and we were let out early because of the war going on in Lebanon. Everyone was gathered around the radio listening to the news, and everyone was saying we were ready to go back to Palestine,” says Imad.
Selon lui, la couverture médiatique arab: According to him, the inaccurate Arab media coverage that followed the start of the 1967 war gave the impression that the war would liberate Palestine. Imad saw Palestinian refugees in Lebanon packing their bags and enthusiastically sharing their plans to return to their homeland. But a few days later, it became clear that Israel had annexed more territory and defeated the Arab forces.
« Cela a été la première déception, je s: “That was the first disappointment, I suppose, at least in my memory. But my parents had seen many more, and me, my generation and my children keep seeing these disappointments caused by the Arab armies, the Arab regimes, the international community, the United Nations, human rights. It’s a series of disappointments,” says Imad.
Imad explique que sa « perception de la: Imad explains that his “perception of pain” as a Palestinian took shape when the civil war broke out in Lebanon. “Palestinians played a central role in that war,” he says. “I lost my first friend. I was 16. He was 16. In the evening, we were playing cards, and the next day we were burying him because shells had fallen on his house and killed him,” Imad recalls, eyes lowered.
“I’ve lost so many friends over the years. I’m speaking here from a personal point of view. But even as a Palestinian who grew up with the politics of the problem, just seeing Israel encroach on Lebanon, on the areas inhabited by Palestinians, assassinating, bombing from planes, I mean, it’s the story of our lives. The pain persists to this day,” he says.
<em>« Nous devons faire entendre notre v: “We have to make our voices heard. No one will do it for us.”
Neda, qui est mariée à Imad, a une histo: Neda, who is married to Imad, has a story similar to his. Her parents, originally from Jenin, in the West Bank, left Palestine “after ’48,” she says. They settled in Jordan hoping to one day return to Palestine. While her parents were never able to go back, Neda was able to travel there with her own children and Imad in 2019, to visit a friend who lived in the Negev.
« Dès que j’ai touché le sol de la Pales: “As soon as I touched Palestinian soil, I felt different. I felt like I was going back to my mother,” she says. “What I regret not visiting is Gaza. Gaza was only 15, 20 minutes away by car. I asked my friend: ‘Can we go?’ She answered: ‘Unfortunately, it’s under siege. It’s impossible to go.’”
« Elle parlait des gens, de leur gentill: “She talked about the people, their kindness, the food, the beach. And I dreamed of going. I couldn’t. Now I regret it because all the good things, it’s… it’s all destroyed,” adds Neda, holding back tears. At these words, the room falls silent. Some sniffle, others wipe away tears, still others sob.
Neda déclare qu’elle doit parler pour mo: Neda says she has to speak up to set an example for her children: “We have to make our voices heard. No one will do it for us. As Palestinians, we have to talk about our stories. We don’t want someone else explaining what we suffer. I owe it to my children. I also have to tell them that we didn’t hide. We didn’t disappear.”
<em>« J’ai perdu beaucoup de membres de: “I lost many family members and friends there. We had a lot of memories. I want others to know that we are aware of their existence, that we haven’t forgotten them.”
Après que les gens se sont ressaisis, Ne: After everyone has composed themselves, Neda passes the microphone to Arwa, a young mother who is studying at university and also works with community organizations. Her parents are Palestinian, but she was born and raised in Saudi Arabia. She obtains Palestinian nationality in 2000. After that, she travels to Palestine for the first time. “Once I was there, everything in my life changed. I felt like myself. I felt I had an identity,” she says.
Elle rappelle que, pour les Palestiniens: She reminds us that, for Palestinians, it didn’t all begin on October 7, 2023. “There were many years, a lot of suffering and a lot of stories before October 7,” explains Arwa.
« Je suis ici parce que toute ma famille: “I’m here because my whole extended family is [in Palestine]. They are under attack right now, but sometimes, when they go online, they see our stories. They see what we posted and what we’re doing. They need to hope that we’re listening to them, that we’re acting and that we’re thinking of them,” says Arwa, tears in her eyes.
« J’ai perdu beaucoup de membres de ma f: “I lost many family members and friends there. We had a lot of memories. I want others to know that we’re thinking of them, that we haven’t forgotten them,” says Arwa.
<em>« Je pense qu’il y a une mécompréhen: “I think there’s a fundamental misunderstanding of the Palestinian experience – if you had been born into this situation, you would do the same things.”
The last person in the circle is Asma. “I don’t know what’s going on, but I’m really overwhelmed,” she begins. After taking a moment to compose herself, she says she was born to a Palestinian father and a Lebanese mother in Beirut, during the Israeli invasion of Lebanon.
« Il y avait des bombardements autour de: “There was bombing around our house. My parents would get into a corner and cover me with their bodies. That’s how I came into the world,” says Asma.
Elle a également constaté les effets de: She also saw the effects of the war while volunteering in a refugee camp in Lebanon when she was 18. “I worked with children. Of course, you notice the garbage, you notice that it’s very, very cramped, and that there are mass graves… but you don’t immediately realize what’s particularly catastrophic about the situation in the camp – which is that at some point, the children become young people and realize they have no future.”
« C’est mon rêve de... J’espère vraiment: “It’s my dream to… I really hope that one day… I can’t even say the sentence, but it’s my dream to go [to Palestine] with my father,” confesses Asma in a trembling voice, fighting back tears.
Elle explique qu’il existe une grande di: She explains that there is a great diversity of Palestinian experiences and backgrounds, some of which were represented during this dialogue evening. “Our experience is so diverse in that sense, in the sense that the Nakba shaped our lives. But that experience, in its scale and its details, is not represented here [in the media]. We’re really put in a box,” says Asma.
Si elle est venue à La Converse pour par: She came to La Converse to share her story in part because she believes people need to see the humanity of Palestinians. “The war in Gaza is not just our problem. It’s something we should look at and recognize ourselves in. It should scare you to see what war looks like right now. If more people understood that we’re not an exception… I think [the war] would be represented differently,” Asma continues.
« Je pense qu’il y a une mécompréhension: “I think there’s a fundamental misunderstanding of the Palestinian experience –. [Palestinians] are not exceptionally violent. We are not exceptionally angry. We are not exceptionally stubborn. Our experiences have shaped us as a people. I think it’s this basic understanding – that at a fundamental level, we are exactly like [non-Palestinians]. (...) I think it’s this fundamental understanding that’s missing here. Like everyone said, I’m here to humanize us,” she concludes.
La question que nous posons à nos invité: The question we put to our guests is: “What hurts you the most right now?”
« Je pense que c’est très simple. Ce qui: “I think it’s very simple. What hurts us right now, immediately, is the genocide. A genocide unfolding before our eyes, on television screens. The Israelis are bombing hospitals, churches, mosques, schools, universities. They are destroying cemeteries. Why? They want to sever every tie between the people and the land,” answers Imad.
Depuis le 7 octobre 2023, plus de 42 000: Since October 7, 2023, more than 42,000 Palestinians have been killed. After a months-long investigation, Amnesty International published <l1>a report</l1> on December 5 concluding that “Israeli authorities are committing the crime of genocide against the Palestinian population in Gaza.” <l2>Francesca Albanese</l2>, the United Nations Special Rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territories, has reached the same conclusion. On November 21, the International Criminal Court (ICC) <l3>issued arrest warrants for Benjamin Netanyahu</l3>, Israel’s prime minister, for war crimes and crimes against humanity. For its part, Israel and its supporters deny all of these accusations.
« L’autre aspect de cette douleur est la: “The other aspect of this pain is neglect… People still have in mind the West’s reaction to what happened in Ukraine. The difference [in reaction] is enormous,” he adds. “Anyone who denies Palestinian pain (…) says more about themselves than about us and our pain. If you deny all this pain, then something is wrong with your vision, your insight and your entire human makeup. Honestly, I mean: How can you?” says Imad.
Nafisa confie son histoire lors de cette: Nafisa shares her story during the evening at La Converse. Photo: Loubna Chlaikhy
Pour Nafisa, une grande partie de sa dou: For Nafisa, much of her pain comes from a feeling of helplessness and the guilt of being safe in Canada while her loved ones suffer. “I’m in touch with my in-laws [in Palestine] every day. As soon as they have internet access, they contact us and tell us about the horrible things happening there every day. Some of them are already dead. All their houses have been destroyed. You see rubble everywhere. Even if you have money, you can’t find anything to buy. They’re hungry, they’re starving too.”
« Quand je mange, je me sens coupable. Q: “When I eat, I feel guilty. When I fall asleep in my bed, I feel guilty. I compare myself to them. They’re waiting for death every moment of their lives. It hurts me so much,” laments Nafisa.
« L’injustice... Je n’ai jamais connu un: “The injustice… I have never known such injustice. It hurts me inside, outside, physically, mentally. I don’t think my life will ever go back to what it was before October 7, with what I’ve seen on social media and what I’ve heard from my loved ones. It’s overwhelming and I can’t explain it. I wish I could, but it’s too much. Sometimes I wish I were there, as if I had never left [Palestine]. At least I would feel like I could do something. What I feel is very, very dangerous for a human being,” says Arwa, with resilience.
Asma ressent l’onde de choc du traumatis: Asma feels the shockwave of intergenerational trauma from her Palestinian father and Lebanese mother, as history seeps into the current conflict. “The other day, I was sitting on the floor with my friends with the news on in the background, and our kids were running around, and I thought, ‘Oh… We’ve become our parents.’ It really shook me, because all I remember of my parents, from one war to the next, is them in front of the television, and [us kids] knowing something is wrong, but not knowing exactly what. You know something is wrong, but you don’t know exactly what. It’s just one generation after another living through one war after another. It’s too much,” says Asma, her eyes wide.
« Ce qui me bouleverse, ce sont les enfa: “What devastates me is the children, of course, and their parents… There’s nothing comparable. During the first months of this genocide, every night when I put my son to bed, I covered him in kisses,” says Asma, miming rocking and kissing an imaginary son, over and over. “What terrifies me is the idea that they’re going to make us disappear,” she adds.
Face à toute cette noirceur, Asma ne man: Faced with all this darkness, Asma is nonetheless quick to point out that Palestinians are not defined solely by their trauma. “I think it’s clear that Palestinians are suffering a great deal, but I also want to say that it’s not what defines us. We are a very proud people. We are proud of ourselves and of the people who came before us. Our experience is painful, but there is also a lot of resilience.”
Après un long dialogue sur ce qui fait m: After a long dialogue about what hurts, we ask them what gives them hope.
Imad voit la fin de la guerre dans un av: Imad sees the end of the war in the near future: “The Israeli project has been a failure from the start. It can only survive with violence and more violence, and by constantly creating more hatred. That hatred eventually catches up with you. These people who commit all these crimes, how can they go back to their families and their homes? I don’t understand. I mean, violence doesn’t only affect the outside. It falls back on you,” he says. He hopes that international attention on Palestine will help put an end to the violence in the region. “Finally, the world is talking about Palestine. I hope it continues,” says Imad.
Fouad souligne la capacité des Palestini: Fouad highlights Palestinians’ ability to create a new vision of the world. “Palestinians have two very powerful weapons. First, a very high level of education. No matter where we go, we can lose money, property, but we will never lose our knowledge. The second very powerful weapon we have is our language. Our language is expressed through music, poets, writers, philosophers, visionaries, and it has also spread among non-Palestinian intellectuals. After October 7, a third very powerful weapon emerged, one we didn’t expect… The emergence of youth – in the streets, in schools, in universities – has been phenomenal. It has forced governments to take measures they had never taken before. I am very, very moved by the number of people protesting who have absolutely no Arab background and who come from all over the world,” explains Fouad.
Selon Neda, le soutien populaire à la Pa: According to Neda, popular support for Palestine can spark change. “I always have hope, but what makes that hope even greater is that university students, my children, are now all informed about what is happening in Palestine. That gives me a lot of hope. My daughter told me: ‘Mom, we are going to free Palestine. This is our generation.’ They’re more organized, they’re doing things and they’re not afraid.”
Le visage de Nafisa s’illumine lorsqu’el: Nafisa’s face lights up when she talks about what she is grateful for, in the midst of her grief. “Look at me! In Canada, my five children received a good education. They have wonderful jobs. I’m surviving. At 78, I’m still working and doing extraordinary work to feel useful in this world. One day, this hypocritical world will wake up to such atrocities and such a genocide and ask itself: ‘How could we have let this happen?’ At the end of the tunnel, there is always a light,” says Nafisa. “Palestinians are a strong people,” she concludes.
Après deux longues heures passées à évoq: After two long hours spent recalling trauma, moving through anger, sadness, outrage, fear and pain, the participants are exhausted. We gather in La Converse’s bright foyer around a feast of traditional Palestinian dishes prepared by a Palestinian grandmother in her seventies, and suddenly the energy returns to the space and people’s eyes light up as they talk about their work, their families and their lives.
Pour Imad, Nafisa, Fouad, Neda, Asma et: For Imad, Nafisa, Fouad, Neda, Asma and Arwa, the political is personal, but their humanity is not up for debate.
